newsitem.title: UK: British explorer sets sights on Antarctic record.
newsitem.headline: British explorer sets sights on Antarctic record.

text.p: British explorer Robert Swan, who has walked to both the North and South Poles, sets off on Thursday in a bid to become the first person to cross all of Antarctica on foot.

After two weeks training on the icy wasteland, Swan, 40, and British adventurers Crispin Day and Geoff Somers will trek 800 miles (1,300 km) from the South Pole to the edge of Antarctica in a 45-day expedition to mark the 50th anniversary of UNESCO.

When the journey ends -- New Year's Eve is the target date -- Swan, who has already walked the other 900 miles (1,450 km) of Antarctica in a 1986 expedition tracing the footsteps of the late British explorer Captain Robert Scott, will fulfil a lifelong dream of becoming the first person to cross the continent on foot.

"It's something I wanted to do ever since I was a kid. I did the South Pole, cracked off the North Pole and now 10 years later I am coming back to finish it off," the special envoy to the director general of UNESCO told Reuters.

After the trek, Swan will join an international team of 35 explorers, aged 16 to 24, for the second phase of the 1.2 million pound ($2 million) privately funded Tandem One Step Beyond Challenge for a month-long trip aboard a Russian icebreaker.

The team, specially chosen from 25 countries and varying backgrounds, will embark from the tip of South America for a month-long voyage that will focus on scientific, cultural, leadership and environmental projects.

"There will be what we call conflict couples," Robin Dunseath, a spokesman for the expedition, said. "From Ireland we have a Catholic and Protestant. There will also be an Israeli and Palestinian, a Russian and a Chechen and a Bosnian Serb, Moslem and Croat."

The young explorers were selected, with the help of government and voluntary organisations in their countries, for their unique backgrounds, potential and enthusiasm. The only condition was that they all speak English.

"They come from all sorts of backgrounds. Some are wealthy, some have no money at all. Some have beaten drugs to get there or been close to militant elements in their own countries," Dunseath said. "We're going to put them in situations where their safety depends on the other person."
Swan and the young explorers will be linked via the Internet (www.onestep.tandem.com) with schoolchildren in their homelands.
At the end of the Antarctic voyage the youths will assess their experiences and what they have learned. If all has gone well, they will be made special junior envoys to UNESCO.
Swan hopes the experience will kindle in the youths leadership qualities and an appreciation of the world's fragile environment which they will convey to people at home. ($1=.6067 Pound)
